original_value: Hyperspectral image (HSI) based detection has attracted considerable attention recently in agriculture, environmental protection and military applications as different wavelengths of light can be advantageously used to discriminate different types of objects. Unfortunately, estimating the background distribution and the detection of interesting local objects is not straightforward, and anomaly detectors may give false alarms. In this paper, a Deep Belief Network (DBN) based anomaly detector is proposed. The high-level features and reconstruction errors are learned through the network in a manner which is not affected by previous background distribution assumption. To reduce contamination by local anomalies, adaptive weights are constructed from reconstruction errors and statistical information. By using the code image which is generated during the inference of DBN and modified by adaptively updated weights, a local Euclidean distance between under test pixels and their neighboring pixels is used to determine the anomaly targets. Experimental results on synthetic and recorded HSI datasets show the performance of proposed method outperforms the classic global Reed-Xiaoli detector (RXD), local RX detector (LRXD) and the-state-of-the-art Collaborative Representation detector (CRD).

result.paraphrase: Hyperspectral image (HSI)-based detection has recently drawn significant attention in agriculture, environmental protection, and military applications, since different wavelengths of light can be used effectively to distinguish object types. However, estimating the background distribution and finding interesting local objects is not easy, and anomaly detectors can produce false alarms. This paper proposes a Deep Belief Network (DBN)-based anomaly detector. The network learns high-level features and reconstruction errors in a way that is not constrained by prior background-distribution assumptions. To lessen contamination from local anomalies, adaptive weights are built from reconstruction errors and statistical information. Using the code image generated during DBN inference and adjusted by adaptively updated weights, the method determines anomaly targets via the local Euclidean distance between pixels under test and their neighboring pixels. Experiments on synthetic and recorded HSI datasets show that the proposed method outperforms the classic global Reed-Xiaoli detector (RXD), the local RX detector (LRXD), and the state-of-the-art Collaborative Representation detector (CRD).
